text: How consistently do customers receive timely follow-up after an inquiry, order, or service request?
options: There is no consistent follow-up process.
Follow-up happens, but it depends on individual effort.
There is a basic follow-up process, but it is not consistently tracked.
Follow-up is structured, reliable, and routinely monitored.

text: How well is customer communication handled when demand increases or issues arise?
options: Communication frequently falls behind or is missed.
We usually respond, but delays and inconsistency are common.
We can generally keep up, though some bottlenecks remain.
Communication remains consistent even during busy periods.

text: How does the business currently generate new customer interest?
options: Mostly by chance, referrals, or word of mouth.
There are occasional marketing efforts, but they are not planned.
Marketing happens regularly, but results are hard to evaluate.
Marketing is deliberate, ongoing, and connected to business goals.

text: How clearly does the business understand what marketing activities are producing results?
options: We do not really know what is working.
We have some impressions, but not enough clarity to guide decisions.
We track some results, but not consistently enough to optimize.
We have enough visibility to make informed marketing decisions.

text: How would you describe the way day-to-day work gets done in the business?
options: Work is mostly reactive and changes from day to day.
Some routines exist, but people still rely heavily on workarounds.
Most key processes are defined, though not always followed consistently.
Core processes are clear, stable, and support predictable execution.

text: How often does the business experience rework, confusion, or avoidable fire-fighting?
options: Very often.
Often enough to create regular disruption.
Sometimes, but the business usually recovers without major difficulty.
Rarely; issues are usually prevented or resolved quickly.

text: How much of leadership or owner time is spent reacting to urgent issues instead of focusing on priorities?
options: Most of the time is reactive.
A large amount of time is reactive.
There is some protected time for priorities, but interruptions still interfere.
Most time is directed toward planned priorities.

text: How effectively does the business protect time for important work rather than constant switching and interruption?
options: There is almost no protection for focused work.
Focused work happens occasionally, but it is easily disrupted.
The business has some structure for priorities, but it is inconsistent.
The business generally protects time and focus for important work.
